events-frames: Trace the light backward from each camera. Were both trips equally long?
An event has one place and one time. Were both flashes at one place?
synchronize: Compare the old and new midpoint between the departure and return clock readings.
Does the full extra time belong to just one leg of this immediate round trip?
light-speed: Test ordinary speed addition against the vacuum light-speed rule for inertial observers.
Changing which way a lamp moves changes some measurements. Which speed do inertial observers assign to vacuum light?
galilean-limit: Could a different sign alone make the measured light speed agree for both forward and backward rays?
Relate clock readings as well as distance readings between the two frames.
proper-time: Find which clock travels between the two events. Should its reading be obtained by multiplying or dividing the lab time by γ?
Were both events at one place in the laboratory? Identify the clock measuring proper time.
light-clock: Draw both the rest-frame and lab light paths with the new mirror spacing.
What quantity sets γ? Did doubling the spacing change that quantity?
length-contraction: Where is the front of the object by the time you record the back?
Does a sharp image guarantee that the endpoint events happened at the same lab time?
simultaneity: Was the spatial separation removed, or was only the direction of the frame velocity reversed?
Find the term containing one factor of frame velocity. Which sign changes when v reverses?
gamma-domain: The sign identifies direction. Which part of the speed, its sign or size, is limited for an ordinary moving frame?
What transformation do you get between two frames with no relative motion?
boost-event: The object is the origin of S′. How would a ruler attached to S′ label that location?
An origin stays at one position over many different clock readings. Which coordinate describes position?
inverse-boost: Compare the value of squared speed for motion toward the left and toward the right.
Is the factor γ determined by a particular clock reading or by relative speed?
velocity-addition: Keep the denominator in the relativistic velocity-addition rule as well as the numerator.
Check whether the light was emitted forward or backward, then use the full transformation.
spacetime-diagram: Did stretching a drawing change the measured times of the actual events?
Compare the graph’s scale labels with the numbers they represent.
interval: Check the sign between time and space terms in the interval used in this lesson.
Try changing frames for a moving clock. Would its time and space separations each be fixed?
separation-types: Does making a frame move closer to light speed change the sign of the interval?
A change of units rescales numbers. Could that turn a possible light signal into an impossible one?
causal-order: Compare events joined by a possible signal with two spacelike-separated events.
Can a change of observer make a signal arrive before it leaves, if that signal travels within the light cone?
piecewise-proper-time: Does reversing direction change the ratio of speed to light speed in magnitude?
Does a clock run backward when a traveler turns and goes another way?
twin-comparison: Would an ideal clock on the same complete path give the same comparison?
Look at the two paths, including who turns around. Do you need an absolute frame to tell the paths apart?
relativistic-doppler: During approach, do successive crests have farther or less far to go before meeting the detector?
The Doppler factor uses both wavefront arrival and clock effects. Is γ alone that factor?
local-inertial: Frame acceleration can change size without changing its direction. Check what is held fixed.
Write proper acceleration = γ³ × lab acceleration and solve for the quantity requested.
relativistic-momentum: Write the mass as well as the speed in p = γmv. Which factor changed?
Does γ depend on mass or speed? Count the changing mass factors.
rest-kinetic-energy: At rest, what energy does a nonzero mass still carry?
Separate the energy of motion from the energy associated with mass.
energy-momentum-invariant: Check which sign in the energy–momentum relation leaves rest energy squared.
Does the relation involve a difference of the quantities or of their squares?
photon-momentum: A photon has no rest mass. Does a beam of light still transfer momentum to a surface?
What happens to E = hf when f changes, and how is photon momentum linked to E?
four-momentum: Turning light around changes its momentum arrow. Does it turn a positive frequency negative?
Try two identical head-on photons. Are their energies being added as arrows or as amounts?
com-frame: Check whether two equal momentum arrows pointing in the same direction already add to zero.
What speeds can an ordinary inertial frame have relative to the laboratory?
inelastic-mass: Did the remaining object keep the energy carried away by the photons?
What determines the remaining mass once both the incoming energy and outgoing radiation are counted?
threshold-energy: Draw the incoming and outgoing momentum arrows in addition to the energy totals.
Can photons of different frequencies have different energies? Which conservation test still needs doing?
charge-current-frames: Current density includes direction. Which way would the charge go past a ruler attached to the moving observer?
Changing your viewpoint changes which way charges move past you. Does it change the charge on each particle?
field-mixing: Which part of the field transformation is already present before changing the sign of the boost?
Look for factors of signed velocity in each transformed component, rather than reversing every arrow.
four-vectors: Check what connects the readings when the observer is changed. Is counting entries enough?
Compare the meaning of an unchanged physical vector with the numbers used to describe it.
covariant-laws: Do conservation laws apply only to the laboratory, or can another inertial observer perform a before-and-after check?
Must both observers agree on the numbers, or can each find that their own before and after totals agree?
equivalence: Which force keeps the spacecraft’s orbit turning around Earth?
Imagine the astronaut and spacecraft falling side by side. What would a scale between them read?
weak-gravity-clocks: Compare the labels assigned to the higher and lower clocks before and after swapping them.
Did any clock start moving in the changed setup, or did the sign of a height difference change?
geodesics: Ask how gravity acts on a freely falling object even when it feels no push from a surface.
Compare a line drawn on a map with what a small accelerometer measures on board.
gravity-limits: Could an accelerating rocket pass through a region with no tidal gravity?
Compare a small laboratory in free fall with predictions across a wide range of heights.
frame-event-capstone: Does the traveler’s own clock visit the return signal’s arrival at the starting point?
Which two events mark the actual start and end of the traveler’s journey?
clock-signal-capstone: Trace the light trip separately from the slower outward trip. Do both speeds change?
The outward distance stayed fixed. Which input to distance ÷ spacecraft speed changed?
collision-capstone: Compare the initial total energy with the proposed rest energy, then do a separate momentum check.
Can an object at rest carry a nonzero total momentum?
relativity-next-tools: What assumptions about gravity and height are needed for this short formula?
Distinguish tiny local measurements from comparing far-apart clocks in a strong field.
